Carpets In Quadri

GeometryAreaConstructions
Game: This is a picture, not a game: the blue middle shape has exactly the same area as the two red pieces together.
How to play: Drag the corners A, B, C and D, or the green point P on side AB; you can also focus a point and use the arrow keys. Tick Hint to see the heights that prove it.
Look for the math

Drag any corner and the blue shape changes size, but it always matches the two red pieces put together. The reason is one shared fraction and one bit of cutting and pasting.

The same fraction on two sides

Point P sits on AB and Q sits on CD so that AP/AB = CQ/CD = r. In points, P = rB + (1-r)A and Q = rD + (1-r)C. The applet keeps the other fraction t = BP/AB = 1-r; drag P and it recomputes t from the distance to B, then places Q the same way on CD. This is why the two sides are always cut in matching ratios.

A triangle split into two heights

Turn the quadrilateral so AB is the base. Drop perpendiculars from C, Q and D to AB and call their lengths c, q and d. Because Q divides CD in the ratio r, its height is the same mixture: q = r·d + (1-r)·c. Every triangle on the base AB has area equal to base times height divided by two, so

Area(AQB) = Area(ADP) + Area(BCP).

Tick Hint to see the orange triangle AQB, the two pink triangles and the green heights QQ', DD' and CC' that give this equation.

Cutting away the corners

Now draw the crossing lines: R is where AQ meets DP, and S is where BQ meets CP. Take the equation above and cut the same two small triangles off both sides. On the left, triangle AQB loses APR and BPS and leaves the blue quadrilateral PSQR. On the right, triangle ADP loses APR and leaves ARD, while BCP loses BPS and leaves BSC. What is left is exactly the claim: Area(PSQR) = Area(ARD) + Area(BSC). No measurement is needed — it is the same area rearranged.

What the test found

The page states this for a convex quadrilateral, and the logic test checks that case: the equality holds at every hundredth of r from 0 to 1 on six fixed shapes (606 configurations) and on 4,000 random convex shapes. It also re-computes the drawing from the applet's own bytecode and agrees on more than 1,500 configurations, including the applet's habit of hiding the carpets when the crossing lines are nearly parallel. For a crossed or dented quadrilateral the equality can fail; the page is right to ask for a convex one, and the status line says so.

Try dragging P close to A, then close to B: the blue carpet shrinks, but the two red pieces shrink with it, so the match never breaks.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
